title: Draupadi
hook: Krishna's wife visits the forest and asks Draupadi for her secret charm, and Draupadi answers with a list of chores and a treasury

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita answered Rama in front of the army, then asked for a fire. Your line was Sita: sort blame into what was in your power and what never was. Did you try it? Now the other epic. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

The question is a little rude, and the guest asks it anyway. The Pandavas are living in the forest, and Krishna comes to visit with his wife Satyabhama. While the men talk, the two women sit together. Satyabhama leans in. Your husbands are heroes, she says, here in paraphrase, and they never cross you. How do you do it? Is it a vow? A mantra? Some herb, some charm? Tell me, so Krishna will be like that with me. Draupadi could laugh. She could be offended. Instead she gives a long answer, and it has no magic in it at all. Today: Draupadi, at home.
screen: `A GUEST IN THE FOREST.` → `WHAT'S YOUR SECRET CHARM?` → `AN ANSWER WITH NO MAGIC IN IT.`

segments.voice: Draupadi starts by refusing the premise. Charms and potions, she says in the epic's Forest Book, are a road to ruin. A husband who learns his wife is working spells on him grows afraid of her, the way a person fears a snake in the house. Then she tells Satyabhama what she actually does, and it reads like a day's work. She sets her pride aside. She rises before the household and sleeps after it. She sees that guests are fed and the servants looked after. And then comes a line some readers stop on. Back when they ruled at Indraprastha, she says, the brothers left the burden of the household's income and spending to her. She alone kept track of it. There's more than one way to hear that. First, it changes the picture. The woman remembered from the dice hall, dragged in by her hair, was also the one who knew where the kingdom's money went. Second, it is practical. Satyabhama wants a shortcut, and Draupadi hands her a routine. Third, it is honestly debated. Some readers hear a model of devotion in this speech. Others hear a portrait of a capable woman running a royal house, in the language her world had for it. Others are uneasy with an ideal built so much around serving. The epic gives the speech and lets readers argue. And one more thing. Draupadi says all this in exile, with no palace and no treasury left. She describes the work she did there from memory, plainly, without complaint.
screen: `CHARMS ARE A ROAD TO RUIN` · `A DAY'S WORK, NOT A SPELL` · `SHE KEPT THE KINGDOM'S ACCOUNTS` · `READERS HEAR IT DIFFERENT WAYS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see the work nobody sees. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one ordinary day in your home, or in a home you grew up in. Who kept track of things? The food, the bills, the guests, the small repairs. Let one person come to mind, maybe you. Don't judge whether it was fair. Just see it, the way Draupadi made Satyabhama see it. With each breath out, let that person be thanked, silently. If you pray, you can name them before God. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi. In the forest, asked for a charm, she gave a list of chores and remembered keeping a kingdom's accounts. Today's word.

Your line: Draupadi. Today, notice one piece of unseen work that keeps a household running, yours or someone else's, and name it out loud to the person who does it. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Hindus meet Draupadi in retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling and theater, and in some regions as a goddess with her own temples and festivals; her conversation with Satyabhama is read in many ways, from a model of devotion to a portrait of a capable queen.

fork.setup: you're Draupadi. Krishna's wife asks for the secret charm that keeps your husbands devoted. what do you say?
options: share a mantra a sage once gave you.
laugh it off and change the subject.
say charms ruin a house, and describe your days.
fork.reveal: she warns that a husband who finds a spell fears his wife like a snake, then gives a long, practical account of her work, down to the treasury.

original.note: Sanskrit: Draupadi, Drupada's daughter. the epic also calls her Panchali, the princess of Panchala.

trapdoor: what you thought: Draupadi is the woman in the dice hall.
what it means: asked for a charm, she describes a day's work and refuses the shortcut.
what a scholar hears: she says the brothers left the household's income and spending to her alone at Indraprastha.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
the year just walked and kept
